newsitem.title: PERU: Peru plans moves ahead of new rebel talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru plans moves ahead of new rebel talks.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori and his Cabinet on Thursday mapped strategy for the next round of face-to-face talks, expected by Saturday, with Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home.

Following his arrival in Lima late on Wednesday from London, Fujimori met for three hours with his Cabinet ministers at Government Palace to be debriefed on Tuesday's meeting, the first between the two sides since Dec. 28.

At that meeting government negotiator Domingo Palermo and Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) second-in-command Rolly Rojas agreed to press on with negotiations to find a solution to the 58-day siege. Palermo told Fujimori he believed talks would go ahead before Saturday afternoon.

"Palermo informed (Fujimori) that he is promoting the second meeting in the sequence of proposed preliminary conversations, which could take place within 48 hours," the government said in a statement around 2 p.m. local time (1900 GMT).

Fujimori has said the talks with Rojas, who goes by the nom de guerre "El Arabe" -- The Arab -- should lead to formal negotiations with rebel leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini. The next talks will take place in the same safe house across the street from the diplomatic compound rented by the Red Cross for Tuesday's talks.

After weeks of deadlock, the resumption of dialogue has marked a breakthrough in the crisis. But with the rebels refusing to give up their demand for the release of hundreds of jailed comrades -- a demand the government flatly rejects -- a peaceful solution is not expected any time soon.

Holed up in the envoy's mansion for over eight weeks, the hostages are showing deepening signs of physical and mental strain. The Red Cross, which is both mediating in the crisis and providing humanitarian aid to the hostages, on Thursday stepped up its medical activities inside the compound.

The organisation laid cables to carry electricity into the fortified embassy residence for the first time since the early days of the siege. Red Cross officials said three specialist doctors would use the electricity for equipment they took into the residence. The officials did not elaborate.

The Red Cross also stocked up on medical supplies, including wheelchairs. The last two hostages released from the compound have been on medical grounds and relatives claim several remaining captives are seriously ill. Aid workers and police say many hostages are being treated for ailments such as hypertension, digestive problems or depression.

Health Minister Marino Costa Bauer said the health of Judge Moises Pantoja, who wrote to his family complaining of arthritic pain, and legislator Gilberto Siura, being treated for cancer, was "delicate," radio reported.
Both sides have sought to avoid harming the hostages but Fujimori has warned he will rule out using force to end the siege only if all the hostages remain unharmed.

Amid fears the crisis could drag on for weeks, Cardinal Augusto Vargas Alzamora, Peru's top Roman Catholic priest, on Wednesday urged the MRTA to end the "agony" of the siege immediately. "Peru would applaud their example. But if they prolong this agony any longer Peru will repudiate them," he told reporters.
Despite local disappointment at the apparent lack of concrete progress at Tuesday's talks, foreign governments reacted with cautious optimism to the dialogue.

The U.S. State Department, viewing it as a "positive step" toward a peaceful solution, said: "The fact that they, after so many weeks, have arrived at the point where they can talk to each other directly in a rational way is a strong indicator that a peaceful solution is possible."
Fujimori's brother and a brother-in-law are among the 72 remaining hostages, who also include two government ministers, the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia and about two dozen Japanese businessmen.
